title: How can we create a durable intergenerational technology community?
status: initial question landscape; no operational validation yet
parent_purpose: Increase the density and variance of useful technological and institutional encounters, expand the ambitions and capabilities reachable by youth and adults, and create a stable community whose value persists across careers and generations.

questions.question: What makes adults return over years, rather than merely volunteer once?
hypotheses: Shared intellectual interests and peer relationships provide intrinsic value.
A recurring cadence and low coordination burden improve continuity.
investigate: Compare communities sustained by member interest with ones dependent on volunteer obligation.
Interview engineers about what would make them attend repeatedly.
questions.first_probe: Host recurring small meetups around an interesting technical topic; observe repeat participation and reasons for returning or not.

questions.question: What kinds of experiences actually expand a youth's landscape of possibilities?
hypotheses: Varied demonstrations, industry talks, projects and informal conversations can reveal unfamiliar possibilities without requiring immediate mastery.
investigate: Compare engineer talks, tours, open build sessions and youth-led demonstrations.
Ask participants what new questions, projects or opportunities they discovered.
questions.first_probe: Invite one engineer to discuss their industry and public technical work, then invite youth to identify something they had not known existed.

questions.question: How do we convert a youth's ambition into access to relevant constituent capabilities?
investigate: Map available expertise, equipment, public resources and affordable substitutes against actual member ambitions.
Identify where coordination or access fails.
questions.first_probe: Help one youth decompose a real project into constituents and connect them to existing people, resources and tools.

questions.question: How can youth take on genuine paid operational responsibility while adults preserve continuity and accountability?
investigate: Study youth employment, supervision, role handoffs, pay funding and appropriate responsibilities.
Find precedents for youth-operated facilities and distinguish paid work from volunteering.
questions.first_probe: Test one bounded operational responsibility with clear support and handoff; arrange compensation and compliant supervision before paid work.

questions.question: How much institutional exposure can be provided through ordinary board activity?
hypotheses: Rotating optional seats reduce exclusivity; participation and questions enable tacit organizational learning.
investigate: Study youth governance participation models and confidentiality boundaries.
Identify accessible transport and safe supervision arrangements.
questions.first_probe: At a future appropriate meeting, invite two or three interested youth, arrange approved transportation/reimbursement, reserve confidential matters, and ask what they found useful.

questions.question: Which functions require a dedicated physical space, and which can begin without one?
investigate: Compare shared venues, partner workshops, mobile makerspaces, libraries and owned facilities.
Estimate recurring costs, supervision, insurance, storage, and access.
questions.first_probe: Run a small project or speaker gathering in a borrowed venue before making any lease commitment.

questions.question: What can be realized at different levels of financing?
investigate: Separate recurring obligations from one-time purchases.
Survey grants, sponsorships, member support, institutional partnerships and in-kind access.
Compare budgets and financial histories from existing organizations.
questions.first_probe: Draft costed scenarios from real venue, equipment, insurance, transportation and staffing inputs when a location and scope are chosen.

questions.question: How do otherwise promising communities become inactive, inaccessible, bureaucratic, or founder-dependent?
investigate: Study failed and sustained makerspaces, volunteer groups, clubs and youth organizations.
Look for recurring causes rather than copying successful organizations' visible structures.
questions.first_probe: Gather contrasting case histories with sources; identify which mechanisms might apply here.

questions.question: How do we broaden participation without selecting only already advantaged or technically confident youth?
investigate: Examine discovery, transport, cost, welcoming culture and entry points for beginners.
Talk to youth and community partners before prescribing solutions.
questions.first_probe: Invite participants with different levels of technical experience to a low-barrier gathering and observe who feels able to participate.

questions.question: How should our accumulated experiences remain useful to future members and personal AIs?
investigate: Preserve original public sources, actual costs, decisions, failed attempts, context and concrete outcomes where useful.
Keep sensitive information in a controlled archive; avoid comprehensive tracking of individuals.
questions.first_probe: After the first real activity, write a short factual account of what happened and what changed in our thinking.

source_families: Professional engineering societies and local chapters
Science clubs, robotics teams, and project communities
Nonprofit annual reports, budgets, governance policies, and failure accounts
Interviews with practitioners and prospective youth participants
comparison_dimensions: Who participates and why they return
Variety of technical encounters and actual projects
Resource ownership, operating costs, staffing, safety
Evidence of outcomes versus stated aspirations
research_strategy.stop_rule: Stop each investigation when it supports a consequential design decision or the next informative experiment; do not wait for an exhaustive survey.
